title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
hookLine: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
carry: raksha: protecting each other is dharma
last: SHIVA IS PLEASED BY THE SMALLEST OFFERING.

lines: A PLATE, A LAMP, A THREAD.
cards: A summer morning, the full moon of the month of Shravana. In homes across India and far beyond, a sister sets out a small plate: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few sweets, and a thread.
Sometimes it's a plain red and gold string. Sometimes it's a glittering thing with a plastic cartoon on it, because her brother is six.
She marks his forehead, circles the lamp in front of his face, ties the thread around his wrist, and pops a sweet in his mouth. He gives her a gift, and a promise: I'll look after you.
Brothers on other continents get their threads in the mail.

teach.b: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a bond. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection.
The thread itself is called a rakhi. It's small enough to snap with two fingers, yet people keep it on for days, because of what it holds.
The best-known story behind it isn't really in the old texts, and it's worth saying so.

People tell that Krishna once cut his finger, and Draupadi, without a second thought, tore a strip from the edge of her sari and tied it around the wound. Krishna was moved, and promised to protect her.
Years later, in the Mahabharata, Draupadi is dragged into a hall full of men and humiliated, and her sari is pulled. And the cloth doesn't end. It keeps coming, and she's covered.
The Mahabharata tells the endless cloth; the torn strip and the promise are how many families tell why.

teach.h: A STRIP OF CLOTH FOR A STRIP OF CLOTH.
teach.b: A strip of cloth for a strip of cloth.
Care offered first, and the promise answers it. Here's the teaching under the thread.
Raksha, protection, is dharma: a duty, not a favor.

teach.h: RAKSHA: PROTECTING EACH OTHER IS DHARMA.
teach.b: And in the telling families love, the one who keeps the promise is God himself; when Draupadi had no one, Krishna covered her. In many families the thread now goes both ways: sisters, cousins, close friends.
That's the week: a birth at midnight, a moon that laughed, nine nights of the Goddess, lamps against the dark, a boy in a fire, a night awake, and now a thread.

how: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists with a lamp, a forehead mark and sweets, and brothers give a gift and a promise of protection; many families now tie it between sisters, cousins and close friends too.

o: a thread tied as a promise of care
a wedding ring traded by cousins
a flower garland for the new year

games.q: what's inside the thread — tap the pairs.
p: tore a strip from her sari
the month of the full moon it's tied

s: the story of Draupadi's torn sari strip is told in the Mahabharata
the Mahabharata tells the endless cloth in the dice hall; the torn strip is how many families tell why.
raksha bandhan means the tie of protection
raksha, protection; bandhan, a tie or bond.
only a sister and a brother can tie a rakhi
Draupadi and Krishna weren't siblings by birth. in many families it goes both ways: sisters, cousins and close friends.

games.q: you're Draupadi. Krishna has cut his finger and it's bleeding. there's no bandage anywhere. what do you do?
o: run to find someone who has cloth.
tear a strip from your sari and tie it on.
tell him to press on it and wait.
games.why: in the story people tell, she tears her own sari without a second thought. care first; Krishna's promise answers it.

practice: Let a face come: a sibling, a child, a parent getting older, a friend having a rough year. Picture tying a thread around their wrist, slowly, the way it's done. If you pray, ask God to protect them, the way a rakhi asks.
Then say it inside, in your own words: I've got you. And think of one small way to keep that promise this week.

wordCard.voice: Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection. Small enough to snap, strong enough to hold a promise.
